newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Wheat pool cut based on bigger crops - AWB.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Wheat pool cut based on bigger crops - AWB.

text.p: The A$10 a tonne reduction in Australia's estimated wheat pool returns for all grades was based on steadily improving crops around the world, Australian Wheat Board general manager, merchandising, Ron Storey, said.
"Basically we've got more grain but at lower prices; overall wheat revenue is probably about unchanged," Storey said.
The statement confirmed the AWB had lifted its estimate of the 1996/97 Australian harvest to 19.0 million tonnes. This would make it Australia's second-largest wheat crop.
The record Australian wheat crop of 22 million tonnes was set in 1983/84. The AWB's previous forecast of the 1996/97 wheat crop was 17.6 million tonnes.
Last week produced news of bigger wheat crops in Canada, the U.S. and Australia, Storey said in a statement.
The market had traded prices downwards right across the board in the last couple of weeks, he said.

A range of U.S. wheats was now priced at about A$220 a tonne, Argentine wheat last week traded at A$193 a tonne fob for February, March delivery, and EU wheat, while not trading in any volume yet, was priced at about A$210, Storey said.

With Australia's bigger crop, its wheat would compete directly with the full range of wheat in 1997, he said. The prices reflected the early 1997 market while Australia's 1996/97 crop would be sold throughout 1997 and into 1998, he said.
While a long way away yet, the mid-1997 market was currently showing a A$15-A$20 discount to the early 1997 values, and the pool return estimates reflect that full year impact, he said.

Last week the market reacted to the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics report that the Australian wheat crop would be about 18.8 million tonnes by immediately trimming prices, Storey said.
"We've delayed announcing our estimated crop size until we've had a chance to ascertain the level of frost damage in Queensland and parts of the Western Australian grain belt," he said.
"We won't know the final outcome until harvest but we now estrimate we'll harvest 19 million tonnes of wheat," he said.
More than two-thirds of the U.S. spring wheat crop had now been harvested and Canada was making good progress with its harvest, he said.
The only uncertainties in the market now were the size of the U.S. corn crop and the fate of the Australian and Argentine wheat crops, he said.
All news so far had been of good crops. The market had digested that and dropped prioces accordingly, he said.
"We have seen some buyers showing reasonable interest at these lower prices and if that interest is sustained we could expect to see some consolidation at these levels," he said.
